cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about tinnitus in time with the pulse, rhythmic ear sounds unrelated to the pulse, and one-sided tinnitus.
We will cover why these situations need a physician's assessment and the audiologist's role in the process.

maddeler.metin: A sound _in time_ with the heartbeat
Often flow in a blood vessel
Sometimes the examiner hears it too

cumleler: Pulsatile tinnitus is tinnitus heard rhythmically, in time with the heartbeat.
People often describe it as a beating, whooshing or humming, as if they could hear their pulse in the ear.
It occurs in only a small share of people with tinnitus, but an underlying cause is more likely to be found.
The sound often comes from irregular, or turbulent, blood flow in a vessel near the ear.
Sometimes the examiner can also hear the sound with a stethoscope or a microphone in the ear canal; this is called objective tinnitus.
This type gets special attention because there may be an underlying vascular or other cause that needs assessment.
In this lesson we will first cover pulsatile tinnitus, then sounds unrelated to the pulse, and then one-sided tinnitus.
In pulsatile tinnitus, the history is very valuable for narrowing down the possible causes.
The person can be asked to feel the pulse at the wrist and say whether the sound keeps the same rhythm.
Ask which ear the sound is in, when it started, and whether it began suddenly or gradually.
If turning the head or gently pressing the neck on the same side reduces the sound, a venous source may be suspected.
Accompanying symptoms such as headache, blurred vision, double vision or ear fullness are also recorded.
The audiologist gathers this information not to make a diagnosis but to pass it on completely to the physician.
The causes of pulsatile tinnitus are roughly grouped as venous, arterial, and abnormal connections between the two.
Venous causes include structural variants such as thinning or a pouch in the wall of the sigmoid sinus.
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, a rise in pressure inside the skull with no known cause, is also a commonly reported cause.
An example of an arterial cause is atherosclerotic narrowing of the carotid artery.
A dural arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal connection between an artery and a vein, and it is a cause that must not be missed.
A paraganglioma, or glomus tumor, a mass rich in blood vessels in or near the middle ear, can also cause pulsatile tinnitus.
Conditions with increased blood flow, such as anemia, an overactive thyroid gland and pregnancy, can also make the sound more noticeable.
In pulsatile tinnitus, otoscopy must never be skipped.
A reddish mass behind the eardrum, especially in the lower half and sometimes pulsating, is a warning sign for a paraganglioma.
Such an appearance should be brought to the physician's attention without delay.
With masses rich in blood vessels, small ripples in time with the pulse may also appear on the tympanogram.
A normal otoscopy, however, does not exclude vascular causes; the physician continues the assessment.
Not every rhythmic sound heard in the ear matches the pulse.
Middle ear myoclonus is an involuntary, rhythmic contraction of the middle ear muscles.
When the stapedius or tensor tympani muscle contracts, the person hears a sound like clicking, fluttering or wing beating.
The sound is unrelated to the pulse; it may be irregular or come in bursts, and is sometimes triggered by outside sounds.
Rhythmic contraction of the soft palate muscles can also cause a clicking sound as the Eustachian tube opens and closes.
A patulous Eustachian tube shows itself with a sound in time with breathing and with hearing one's own voice loudly.
In some of these conditions, the examiner can also hear the sound.
An immittance instrument can be used to observe middle ear myoclonus.
With the probe in the ear canal, a time-based admittance recording is made without a stimulus; the reflex decay screen can be used for this.
Because muscle contractions move the eardrum, short, rhythmic admittance ripples may be seen in the recording.
If these ripples coincide with the sounds the patient hears, the finding is supported.
Ripples in time with breathing may suggest a patulous Eustachian tube; the findings are passed to the physician.
Unilateral tinnitus is tinnitus heard in only one ear, or clearly more on one side.
It needs special attention, especially when it comes with asymmetric hearing loss on the same side.
Here the right ear is normal; the left has high-frequency sensorineural thresholds 25 to 30 dB worse, confirmed by masked bone conduction.
By a commonly used criterion, a difference of 15 decibels or more at two adjacent frequencies is considered significant asymmetry.
Such a picture needs a physician's assessment for retrocochlear causes such as vestibular schwannoma.
One-sided tinnitus may even be the first noticed symptom of an asymmetric hearing loss.

cumleler: But this changes if the tinnitus is one-sided or pulsatile, or if there are focal neurological signs or asymmetric hearing loss.

cumleler: The same guideline recommends referral for further assessment of tinnitus with unilateral or asymmetric hearing loss.
The physician decides on the type and timing of imaging; the audiologist's job is to recognize the finding and report it accurately.
This approach aims to avoid unnecessary imaging while making sure important causes are not missed.
Some tinnitus presentations cannot wait.
If tinnitus comes with sudden hearing loss, the person is referred to a physician without delay.
Neurological symptoms such as facial weakness, speech problems, double vision or sudden severe dizziness are an emergency.
If the person expresses hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm because of tinnitus, they are referred to mental health support right away.
If pulsatile tinnitus comes with a sudden severe headache or vision loss, immediate referral is also needed.
In these situations, do not wait to complete the test battery.
Let us summarize the audiologist's pathway in pulsatile or one-sided tinnitus, step by step.
First, a detailed history is taken, and the eardrum is examined carefully with otoscopy.
Then pure tone and speech audiometry, tympanometry and acoustic reflex tests are done.
The findings are recorded in a clear report, together with the patient's own words describing the sound.
Finally, the person is referred to a physician; decisions on diagnosis and imaging belong to the physician.
This order makes sure no step is skipped and the physician receives complete information.

cumleler: A clinical tip: when referring, do not frighten the patient, but do not downplay the situation either.
For example, you can say that a physician's assessment is a standard step to clarify the cause in this type of tinnitus.
In the referral letter, include the quality of the sound, its side, whether it matches the pulse, and the audiological findings.
This information helps the physician choose the right investigation.
Pulsatile tinnitus is in time with the pulse and often points to a vascular source; it needs a physician's assessment.
Middle ear myoclonus shows itself with irregular clicking sounds unrelated to the pulse.
One-sided tinnitus, especially with asymmetric hearing loss, is referred to look for retrocochlear causes.
Sudden hearing loss, neurological symptoms and thoughts of self-harm call for referral without waiting.
